How the batch was triaged: /work/task.py (a Jev Harness script) reads all 1000 events and sorts each one into one of six labels: PAGE, NONPROD, RESOLVED, INTERNAL, DRILL_OR_FALSE_ALARM or NOT_INCIDENT. Each event is judged on its latest statement, and only PAGE events go into the report. The model's instructions spell out the tricky cases: QA, pre-prod and perf-test environments count as non-production; mitigated or back-to-baseline means resolved; admin-console or back-office impact only is internal; game days and broken synthetic probes are excluded; postmortems and policy questions are not incidents.

The first run had a problem: one provider batch failed, so 29 events were never judged. That report still passed with 280 ids. I added two fixes to the script: an automatic second pass for any unjudged events, and a resume={"resume": true} input that re-judges only the leftover events and merges them into the existing report. Running resume judged those 29 cheaply, added 9 real pages, and left nothing unjudged. It also checked the new merge code end to end. The automatic second pass did not run in either run, so it hasn't been tested live. Both runs passed.

For future batches, /work/README.md explains how to rerun the procedure and what it costs, which is about 37 requests (roughly 460k input tokens) per 1000 events. Each run also writes /work/report.json.details.json; check that its review_ids list is empty before trusting the report. The first run's files are kept as /work/report.run1.json and /work/report.run1.details.json.
final_output.approach_reason: I used Jev's batched judging rather than hand-written rules. The events are free-text and full of corrections ('Correction:', 'Update:', 'Follow-up:'), mixed environment hints and decoy phrases, so matching keywords would break on the varied wording of future batches. One typed question with clear labels can be rerun daily, and it judged all 1000 events in about 15 seconds. The resume path recovers a failed batch for about 1/40th of a full rerun's cost.
